questions.question: Which revolutionary scientific work did Charles Darwin publish on 24 November 1859, introducing the theory of evolution by natural selection?
options: Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation
Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature
questions.explanation: Darwin published On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection in November 1859 selling out all 1250 copies on the first day.

questions.question: What was the popular name of the giant cast-iron and plate-glass building designed by Joseph Paxton in Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition of 1851?
questions.explanation: Punch magazine christened Joseph Paxton prefabricated glass and iron exhibition hall the Crystal Palace.

questions.question: In which year was the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood founded in London by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, William Holman Hunt, and John Everett Millais?
questions.explanation: Seven young artists and writers formed the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood at Millais parents house in Gower Street in September 1848.

questions.question: In Alfred Tennyson's Arthurian ballad 'The Lady of Shalott', the sight of which knight riding toward Camelot causes the Lady to look directly out her window?
questions.explanation: Seeing bold Sir Lancelot flash into her crystal mirror the Lady leaves her web looks down to Camelot and brings the curse upon herself.

questions.question: Which 1832 poem by Alfred Tennyson depicts Ulysses's mariners landing on an island where eating an enchanted plant makes them crave only rest?
questions.explanation: Inspired by Book IX of Homer Odyssey Tennyson The Lotos-Eaters contrasts heroic toil with languorous escapism.

questions.question: Which 1855 experimental work did Alfred Tennyson subtitle 'A Monodrama', narrating a morbid speaker's love, fatal duel, madness, and departure for the Crimea?
questions.explanation: Tennyson published Maud A Monodrama in 1855 and considered it his own favorite poem to read aloud.

questions.question: Which short 1889 lyric did Alfred Tennyson request be placed at the very end of all editions of his poetry as his farewell meditation on death?
questions.explanation: Composed while crossing the Solent to the Isle of Wight in October 1889 Crossing the Bar closes every collected edition of Tennyson.

questions.question: Which Italian Renaissance nobleman is the cold, possessive speaker of Robert Browning's 1842 dramatic monologue 'My Last Duchess'?
options: Alfonso II d'Este, Duke of Ferrara
questions.explanation: Subtitled Ferrara the poem is spoken by Alfonso II fifth Duke of Ferrara regarding his first wife Lucrezia de Medici.

questions.question: Along which German river is the town of Hamelin situated in Robert Browning's famous 1842 narrative poem 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin'?
questions.explanation: Written for Willie Macready the poem notes that the deep and wide River Weser washes the southern wall of Hamelin town.

questions.question: What subtitle is given to Robert Browning's 1855 dramatic monologue 'Andrea del Sarto', in which the painter reflects that 'a man's reach should exceed his grasp'?
questions.explanation: Published in Men and Women 1855 Andrea del Sarto Called The Faultless Painter portrays an artist of technical perfection who lacks spiritual fire.

questions.question: With which immortal question does Sonnet 43—the most famous lyric in Elizabeth Barrett Browning's 'Sonnets from the Portuguese' (1850)—begin?
options: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
When our two souls stand up erect and strong
If thou must love me, let it be for nought
How do I love thee? Let me count the ways
questions.explanation: Sonnet 43 is the penultimate sonnet in Elizabeth Barrett Browning forty-four-sonnet sequence to Robert Browning.

questions.question: From which seventeenth-century book by Joseph Glanvill did Matthew Arnold draw the legend of the impoverished Oxford student in 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (1853)?
questions.explanation: Arnold took the story of the Oxford scholar who joined the gypsies to learn their mental arts from Joseph Glanvill 1661 treatise The Vanity of Dogmatizing.

questions.question: Which 1853 blank-verse epic episode by Matthew Arnold, drawn from the Persian 'Shahnameh', recounts a tragic duel in which a father unknowingly slays his son?
questions.explanation: Arnold published Sohrab and Rustum An Episode in his 1853 Poems illustrating his preface call for grand objective action.

questions.question: In Dante Gabriel Rossetti's Pre-Raphaelite poem 'The Blessed Damozel' (1850), what symbolic numbers of lilies and stars adorn the maiden in heaven?
options: One lily in her hand and twelve stars in her hair
Five lilies in her hand and five stars in her hair
Seven lilies in her hand and three stars in her hair
Three lilies in her hand and seven stars in her hair
questions.explanation: Stanza 1 states She had three lilies in her hand And the stars in her hair were seven.

questions.question: Which 1865 lyrical drama in classical Greek form earned Algernon Charles Swinburne immediate acclaim for its sweeping choral meters?
questions.explanation: Swinburne published Atalanta in Calydon in 1865 featuring the famous chorus Before the beginning of years.

questions.question: Under what famous single-word pen name did the young Charles Dickens publish 'Sketches' (1836) and 'The Pickwick Papers'?
questions.explanation: Derived from a family nickname for his younger brother Augustus Moses Dickens used the pseudonym Boz for his early journalism and fiction.

questions.question: Which 1837–1839 novel by Charles Dickens fiercely satirized the cruel parish workhouse system created by the New Poor Law of 1834?
questions.explanation: Serialized in Bentley Miscellany Oliver Twist or The Parish Boy Progress exposed the starvation and cruelty of the 1834 Poor Law workhouses.

questions.question: Who is the deceased business partner whose ghost, bound in heavy chains of cash-boxes and ledgers, visits Ebenezer Scrooge first in 'A Christmas Carol' (1843)?
questions.explanation: Dead for seven years Jacob Marley visits Scrooge on Christmas Eve to warn him of the three Spirits.

questions.question: Which 1849–1850 semi-autobiographical novel did Charles Dickens affectionately call his 'favourite child' in his 1867 preface?
questions.explanation: Drawing on his own childhood toil at Warren Blacking Factory and his courtship of Maria Beadnell Dickens called David Copperfield his favourite child.

questions.question: Which two European capitals are the 'two cities' of Charles Dickens's 1859 historical novel set before and during the French Revolution?
questions.explanation: A Tale of Two Cities alternates between peaceful London and revolutionary Paris during the Reign of Terror.

questions.question: Which dissolute English barrister goes willingly to the guillotine in place of Charles Darnay at the climax of 'A Tale of Two Cities' (1859)?
questions.explanation: Out of love for Lucie Manette Sydney Carton drugs Darnay in prison and dies at the guillotine speaking his famous prophetic words.

questions.question: Which murder-mystery novel was left only half-finished by Charles Dickens when he died suddenly at Gad's Hill Place in June 1870?
questions.explanation: Only six of the planned twelve monthly parts of The Mystery of Edwin Drood were written leaving the fate of Edwin Drood unsolved.

questions.question: Who is the scheming, ruthlessly ambitious green-eyed governess who serves as the central protagonist of Thackeray's 'Vanity Fair' (1847–1848)?
questions.explanation: Rebecca Sharp the daughter of an impoverished artist and a French opera girl climbs Victorian society by her wits.

questions.question: In Charlotte Brontë's 'Jane Eyre' (1847), what is the name of Mr. Edward Rochester's brooding manor house where Jane serves as governess?
questions.explanation: Jane Eyre leaves Lowood School to teach Adèle Varens at Thornfield Hall where Bertha Mason is confined on the third floor.

questions.question: Which 1849 social novel by Charlotte Brontë is set in Yorkshire during the Luddite textile machinery disturbances of 1811–1812?
questions.explanation: Published in October 1849 Shirley depicts the mill-owner Robert Moore confronting Luddite frame-breakers during the Napoleonic Wars.

questions.question: Which 1848 debut novel by Elizabeth Gaskell, subtitled 'A Tale of Manchester Life', portrays the working-class desperation of a Chartist weaver?
questions.explanation: Gaskell published Mary Barton anonymously in October 1848 arousing deep sympathy for the industrial workers of Manchester.

questions.question: Which landmark 1857 biography did Elizabeth Gaskell write at the request of Patrick Brontë to honor and defend her deceased friend?
options: Lives of the Queens of England
questions.explanation: Gaskell 1857 The Life of Charlotte Brontë is one of the greatest English biographies establishing the tragic legend of Haworth.

questions.question: Which 1863 moral fairy tale by Charles Kingsley follows a young chimney sweep named Tom who is transformed into an aquatic creature?
questions.explanation: Subtitled A Fairy Tale for a Land-Baby Kingsley 1863 book combined satire on child labor with Christian evolutionary parables.

questions.question: What is the name of the fictional English county that forms the setting for Anthony Trollope's six-novel clerical series (1855–1867)?
questions.explanation: Beginning with The Warden 1855 and Barchester Towers 1857 Trollope Chronicles of Barsetshire are set in the cathedral county of Barsetshire.

questions.question: In George Eliot's 'Silas Marner' (1861), what golden-haired toddler wanders into the weaver's cottage and replaces his stolen hoard of gold?
questions.explanation: Named Hephzibah or Eppie after Silas mother and sister the unacknowledged child of Godfrey Cass redeems Silas Marner from isolation.

questions.question: Who is the idealistic young heroine of George Eliot's 'Middlemarch' (1871–1872) who makes the tragic mistake of marrying the elderly scholar Edward Casaubon?
questions.explanation: Compared in the Prelude to a modern Saint Teresa Dorothea Brooke weds the arid pedant Casaubon before later marrying Will Ladislaw.

questions.question: Who is the narcissistic, self-centered baronet from whom Clara Middleton struggles to break her engagement in George Meredith's 1879 novel 'The Egoist'?
questions.explanation: Sir Willoughby Patterne of Patterne Hall embodies comic male egoism and is ultimately forced to marry the weary Laetitia Dale.

questions.question: What was the real name of the Oxford mathematics lecturer who published 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' (1865) under the pseudonym Lewis Carroll?
questions.explanation: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson of Christ Church Oxford created the pseudonym Lewis Carroll by Latinizing and anglicizing his first two names.

questions.question: Which 1869 historical romance by R. D. Blackmore narrates farmer John Ridd's love for a noblewoman raised by seventeenth-century Exmoor outlaws?
questions.explanation: Subtitled A Romance of Exmoor Blackmore 1869 novel Lorna Doone became one of the most beloved regional romances of the Victorian era.

questions.question: What ancient Anglo-Saxon kingdom's name did Thomas Hardy revive for the semi-fictional southwest England setting of his major novels?
questions.explanation: Hardy first introduced the geographical name Wessex in Chapter 50 of Far from the Madding Crowd in 1874 centered on his native Dorset.

questions.question: Who is the independent female farm-owner in Thomas Hardy's 'Far from the Madding Crowd' (1874) courted by Gabriel Oak, Boldwood, and Sergeant Troy?
questions.explanation: Inheriting her uncle Weatherbury farm Bathsheba Everdene weds the reckless Sergeant Troy before finally marrying the faithful shepherd Gabriel Oak.

questions.question: Which impulsive hay-trusser sells his wife Susan and baby daughter for five guineas at a country fair in the opening chapter of Hardy's 'The Mayor of Casterbridge' (1886)?
questions.explanation: Intoxicated on rum-laced furmity at Weydon-Priors fair Michael Henchard auctions off his wife and child before swearing a twenty-one-year oath of abstinence.

questions.question: In Robert Louis Stevenson's 'Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde' (1886), who is the sober London lawyer through whose eyes most of the mystery is investigated?
questions.explanation: Mr Gabriel John Utterson is Dr Jekyll lawyer and loyal friend who preserves and reads Lanyon and Jekyll final confessions.

questions.question: In which 1887 novel, printed in 'Beeton's Christmas Annual', did Sir Arthur Conan Doyle first introduce Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson?
questions.explanation: Doyle introduced Holmes and Watson sharing rooms at 221B Baker Street in A Study in Scarlet published in November 1887.

questions.question: Which 1901 picaresque novel by Rudyard Kipling follows the orphaned Irish boy Kimball O'Hara accompanying an aged Tibetan lama across British India?
questions.explanation: Published in October 1901 Kim portrays Kimball O Hara torn between the British secret service Great Game and the lama spiritual quest.

questions.question: What is the name of the human child raised by the wolf pack in the Indian jungle in Rudyard Kipling's 'The Jungle Book' (1894)?
questions.explanation: Rescued from the tiger Shere Khan by Father Wolf and Mother Wolf Mowgli is taught the Law of the Jungle by Baloo and Bagheera.

questions.question: Which 1898 scientific romance by H. G. Wells depicts the invasion of Victorian England by Martians who are ultimately destroyed by earthly bacteria?
options: The First Men in the Moon
questions.explanation: Wells 1898 novel The War of the Worlds lands Martian cylinders on Horsell Common in Surrey to critique British imperial complacency.

questions.question: Which 1894 anti-romantic comedy by George Bernard Shaw features the pragmatic 'chocolate-cream soldier' Captain Bluntschli and takes its title from Virgil's 'Aeneid'?
questions.explanation: Included in Plays Pleasant 1898 Arms and the Man debunks military and romantic idealism through the Swiss mercenary Bluntschli.

questions.question: In Oscar Wilde's novel 'The Picture of Dorian Gray' (1890/1891), what is the name of the moralistic painter who creates the fatal portrait of Dorian?
questions.explanation: Basil Hallward paints the masterpiece of Dorian Gray and is later murdered by Dorian when he sees the corrupted canvas in the schoolroom.

questions.question: Which poignant 1898 poem did Oscar Wilde write after his release from prison, commemorating the execution of Royal Horse Guards trooper Charles Thomas Wooldridge?
questions.explanation: Published initially under Wilde prison cell number C.3.3. The Ballad of Reading Gaol contains the refrain Yet each man kills the thing he loves.

questions.question: Which 1893 religious ode by the Catholic poet Francis Thompson portrays God's grace as an unwearying celestial pursuer following the fleeing soul?
questions.explanation: Opening I fled Him down the nights and down the days Francis Thompson The Hound of Heaven was published in his 1893 Poems.

questions.question: Which stoic 1875 lyric by William Ernest Henley, written while recovering from leg amputation surgery, concludes 'I am the master of my fate, / I am the captain of my soul'?
questions.explanation: Written in the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary under Joseph Lister care Henley poem was published in his 1888 Book of Verses and later titled Invictus.

questions.question: Which 1889 comic masterpiece by Jerome K. Jerome narrates a boating holiday up the Thames taken by J., Harris, George, and the dog Montmorency?
options: Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow
questions.explanation: Subtitled To Say Nothing of the Dog Jerome K Jerome 1889 book intended as a serious Thames guide became an enduring classic of Victorian humor.

questions.question: Which illustrated quarterly periodical, published in London from 1894 to 1897 with Aubrey Beardsley as its first art editor, epitomized the decadent 'Nineties'?
questions.explanation: Published by Elkin Mathews and John Lane from April 1894 The Yellow Book became the symbol of British fin-de-siècle aestheticism.

questions.question: In which year did Queen Victoria die at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight after a reign of nearly sixty-four years, closing the Victorian Period?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria died on 22 January 1901 and was succeeded by her eldest son King Edward VII.
